name: Red Lilac Purple
lede: Red Lilac Purple is a pale, faintly pinkish grey-lilac from Patrick Syme's colour nomenclature, number 43 among his purples and illustrated by the pale spots on a peacock butterfly's wing.

sections.title: Where the name comes from
sections.body:
Red Lilac Purple belongs to the colour nomenclature of Patrick Syme, who in 1814 adapted Werner's list of colours into a reference book for naturalists [1]. Syme was a student of botany and entomology as well as an artist. His first edition grew the earlier list of 80 mineral colour terms to 108, adding two new groups, orange and purple, and the second edition of 1821 reached 110 [1].

Syme took *lilac* from the English edition of Willdenow's botany textbook and made two varieties of it: bluish lilac purple and red lilac purple [1]. The first word is a modifier: this is the lilac that leans toward red. Within his purples it is number 43 [2].

Lilac is still a live question in color naming [7]. A 2015 online experiment by Mylonas and MacDonald argued that English should count *lilac*, together with turquoise, among its basic color terms, a proposal that remains contested [7].

sections.title: Butterfly, primrose, mineral
sections.body:
Syme gave every color three living examples, one each from the animal, vegetable and mineral worlds, so that a naturalist could match a specimen against the chart [1]. For Red Lilac Purple, the animal is the light spots on the upper wings of the peacock butterfly [2]. The plant is red lilac itself and the pale purple primrose, and the mineral is lepidolite [2].

The chart stayed in use in the field long after Syme [3]. Baty's chapter on its place in botany lists plants set beside this number, among them the petal of the violet wood-sorrel, *Modecca lobata* and the arctic poppy [3].

sections.title: An aged swatch
sections.body:
Syme's colours were painted by hand, and paint changes. Ridgway complained in 1886 that few of Syme's colours still matched their intended tints, and that names drawn from familiar things, lilac among them, were arbitrary [4]. The swatch on this page is an approximation taken from an aged chart, so it shows what the paper looks like now, not the butterfly of 1814 [5].

It is a light, cool-leaning grey with only a trace of purple, and its lightness is 76 out of 100 [5]. In ISCC-NBS terms it falls in block 232, light purplish gray [5]. The nearest named color in our library is [[silver]], 4.6 units away, while [[lilac]] itself is a far more colorful purple [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a screen color within six units of Red Lilac Purple covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 440 works, or 1.85 per cent [6]. It is a light color: in 94 per cent of those paintings it plays a highlight role in the lightness order, not a middle or shadow one [6].

[[painter:gustav-klimt|Klimt]] is the strongest single painter. Nine of his 50 paintings in the archive carry it, nearly ten times the archive's rate, and the largest cover is a panel of his *Beethoven Frieze*, dated 1901, where it fills 83 per cent of the image [6]. Austria shows the highest national lift, 9 of 121 paintings, or four times the average [6]. By century it is 2.4 times as common in the 1900s as across the archive [6].

The earliest example is [[painting:cma-159234|a painted crucifix with scenes of the Passion]], dated 1230, where it covers 68 per cent [6]. Two caveats travel with every number. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test: a pale grey this common is often a ground, a wall or a shadow, not a lilac [6].

questions.q: What three kinds of living example did Syme give for each color in his nomenclature?
choices: An animal, a plant and a mineral
A flower, a gem and a pigment
A painter, a poet and a dyer
questions.answer: An animal, a plant and a mineral

questions.q: Which animal does Syme use to show Red Lilac Purple?
choices: The pale spots on a peacock butterfly's upper wings
The breast of a pied wagtail
The back of a kittiwake gull
The wing of a blue morpho
questions.answer: The pale spots on a peacock butterfly's upper wings

questions.q: True or false: Syme invented his whole color list from nothing.

openers: Syme matched Red Lilac Purple to the pale spots on a peacock butterfly's wings, to a primrose and to the mineral lepidolite.
Syme's list grew from 80 mineral colors to 108 in 1814 by adding orange and purple groups.
Look for it in the pale eye spots on the upper wings of a peacock butterfly: a light, cool grey with a hint of lilac.

issues: Softened 'trained as' to 'student of botany and entomology, and an artist' per Baty.
